title: Chamier: absent-capable honors are due; genuflection, greeting, and gifts to the needy are not
source_text: XXXII. Id inter alios observat Daniel Chamierus. Postquam enim constituit eum honorem qui Sanctis deferendus est, esse eundem specie, cum eo quem vivis deferri oportet, & ab eo differre tantum intensione & remissione, quae varios quidem gradus efficiunt, sed non variant species: notat distinguendum esse quoad actus honoris illius. Quosdam enim Sanctis deberi: ut qui deferri possunt quibuslibet hominibus absentibus. At quaecunque praesentibus tantum deferuntur, ut genuflexiones, salutationes, inclinationes, similiaque multa, ea non deberi Sanctis: & multo magis quae indigentibus, ut vestes, lumina, panem, vinum. Panstratia tom. 2. lib. 19. cap. 2. num. 20.
pass_a_gloss: Daniel Chamier, among others, observes this. For after he has established that the honor to be paid to the Saints is the same in species as that which ought to be paid to the living, and differs from it only in intensity and remission, which indeed make various degrees but do not vary the species, he notes that one must distinguish as to the acts of that honor. For some are owed to the Saints: namely those which can be paid to any men who are absent. But whatever is paid only to those present, such as genuflections, greetings, bows, and many similar things, these are not owed to the Saints: and much more those things which are for the needy, such as clothes, lights, bread, and wine. Panstratia, volume 2, book 19, chapter 2, number 20.
pass_b_english: Chamier holds that honor of the Saints is the same in kind as honor of the living, and differs only by being stronger or weaker.
Degree does not change the species.
Acts that can be paid to people who are absent are due; genuflection, greeting, and bowing, which need presence, are not.
Still less are gifts for the needy, such as clothes, lights, bread, and wine.

choices.why: The test of a lawful act is whether it can be paid without presence.
rejected: every courtesy paid to the living
